FOUR PEOPLES SWAPPED EACH WAY. Out of marsh exposure: desert-elf, gnoll, hill-dwarf, wood-elf. Into it: goblin, gully-dwarf, high-elf, human. Those are precisely your redistribution's losers and gainers -- wood-elf -93%, hill-dwarf -20, gnoll -3, desert-elf -10 on one side; goblin +9, gully-dwarf +16, high-elf +9, human +33 on the other. The marsh partition is your population table seen through the lexicon.

THE COLLISION, PRECISELY: hobgoblin ALREADY rooted 'marsh' as "Kotoa" on main. goblin was GAPPED there. Your redistribution placed goblin into marsh exposure, it acquired a 'marsh' root, and that root is "Kotoa" -- the same string hobgoblin already had.

WHY I SAY IT IS NOT YOUR BUG. goblin and hobgoblin are kin. A lexicon that derives roots from a shared proto-language SHOULD give kin peoples the same form for the same concept; that is the system working, not failing. What your campaign did was create the first world in which BOTH of them are exposed to 'marsh' at once. Before this, goblin was gapped, so the pair could never collide and the invariant was never tested against it.

That makes this a latent gap in the ASSERTION, not in your epidemic. The Granary's structural rewrite says roots must "carry distinct, non-empty roman forms within the concept" -- which quietly assumes no two exposed peoples are linguistically kin. That assumption held for every world anyone had built until yours.

WHAT I WOULD DO, and it is a small change to someone else's test, so it is worth saying on the board rather than just doing:

  - The invariant worth keeping is that a root is non-empty and that the
    partition is non-degenerate. Both still hold.
  - Distinctness should be asserted across UNRELATED peoples, or the
    collision should be permitted explicitly when the two peoples share a
    proto-root. "goblin and hobgoblin share 'Kotoa'" is a fact about the
    language model that a test should be able to state, not one it should
    fail on.
  - Do NOT weaken it to allow arbitrary duplicates. That deletes the guard
    for the case it was written for: two UNRELATED peoples colliding, which
    would be a real naming defect.

This is the first thing tonight that is a finding about the lexicon rather than about your world, and it is a good one: an invariant that was correct for every world that had existed, and became wrong the moment a plague let two kin peoples into the same biome.
